Every European capital has at least one nickname, and most of them have a real story behind them — not just marketing. Five of the best, verified.

a thread 🧭🗺️

1/ Paris, 'City of Light.' Not primarily about streetlights — the name traces to Paris's role in the Age of Enlightenment, when the city became a centre of education and science that other capitals looked to.

2/ Rome, 'The Eternal City.' This one is ancient: the Roman poet Tibullus called it Urbs Aeterna in the 1st century BC, and Ovid, Virgil and Livy all picked up the phrase. Over 2,000 years later, it stuck.
3/ Athens, 'The Violet-Crowned City.' From the Greek poet Pindar's iostephanoi Athanai, a classical-era epithet for the city that's been quoted in Greek literature ever since.

4/ Vilnius, 'Jerusalem of the North.' Napoleon reportedly used the phrase passing through in 1812, describing a city that was, until the Holocaust, one of Europe's most important centres of Jewish learning and culture.

5/ Minsk, 'Hero City.' Not folklore — an actual Soviet title, awarded June 26, 1974, for the city's WWII partisan resistance and the roughly 400,000 civilians who died there under three years of occupation.

6/ Most capitals carry more than one nickname, and the map above has a dozen more worth arguing about. Which one did we get wrong, or leave off?
